newsitem.title: USA: U.S. copper cathode spot premiums feel the squeeze.
newsitem.headline: U.S. copper cathode spot premiums feel the squeeze.

text.p: Spot premiums on copper cathode in the U.S., the world's biggest red metal consumer, are feeling the pinch, but the jury was still out over just how long the modest spike will last, dealers said.
Premiums on cathode in the North East and Midwest have risen to 2.75 to 3.50 cents per pound over spot month COMEX which traded at 119.50 cents per pound midmorning Friday.
Earlier in the year premiums were 2.75 to 3.00 cents. Few believed business of any great volume was being done at the upper end of the new range.

"I think predominantly the reason for these premiums was the fact there was a large portion of cathode from Western states going all the way up to Connecticut. The freight alone was going to push the premium higher," the producer official said. "It's just a short-term situation."
A cathode buyer for an East Coast mill said: "I don't think the premiums will go up any further, but I think they will stay up at these levels for most of the year."
Brokers noted the weaker arbitrage forced some to ship the metal from the West to the East Coast.
Others felt liquidation by Cerro Sales of its long, nearby positions may be affecting premiums as it pushes June COMEX into contango with July despite an LME backwardation.
Cerro, which will be merged with an MG subsidiary from June 1, was expected to complete the liquidation this week.
"Anyone with as big a book as Cerro in the physical market is bound to have an influence," a senior broker said.
Dealers expected June demand for copper in the U.S. to remain strong, particularly in the Northeast. "I think copper will be coming out of warehouses at a rapid clip," a broker said.
But one South West producer said: "In spite of the fact that consumption has been good, particularly in the Midwest, the signs are definitely there that things are quieting down."
Another producer countered that demand for rod was very good but tubing was likely to remain fairly flat this year. No unusual slackening in demand was on the horizon, he added.
Tension, if not tightness in the market may well ease.
Earlier this week Rio Tinto's Kennecott Utah Copper Corp said its big smelter was back on stream and expected to hit capacity later in the year.
There was also relief that workers at Noranda Inc's Gaspe operation ratified a new labor deal this week ahead of a planned shutdown at its Horne smelter.
Inco, which produces some copper at Sudbury, also looked more likely to see a new labor deal ratified this week end without a strike. Unions accepted a tentative deal Friday.

Once Kennecott is fully on stream the company will be integrated and there will be some displacement in the blister market, dealers said. Kennecott had been selling some blister to traders who, in turn, sold to other U.S. refiners.

"I think there will be more blister coming in from Mexico first, and then Chile," a concentrates dealer said. "But I don't see any big difference in blister prices and no new fresh business between now and the end of the year."

But others said Kennecott's start-up may lead to a tightening of the blister market in the Southwest where much of the refining capacity is located. "Logically, refining charges have to go down in the U.S.," a merchant said.

U.S. blister refining charges are about $150 to $180 per tonne, about halfway between the low prices of $200 in Europe where there is stiff competition from cheap scrap, and Asia where refining charges are expensive at $100 or below.
The copper blister and concentrates market is also largely on hold as talks between miners and Japanese smelters are due to start over next year's contracts.
